title: A tenth
hook: the tradition of giving a tenth of income
tomorrow: Noa has her tenth. a check, or something better?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Akiva's broom: the visit that heals is presence and help together. Hands of the community. Hands can carry money too.
screen: `HANDS OF THE COMMUNITY.` → `HANDS CARRY MONEY TOO.`

segments.voice: A first paycheck has a weight to it, even as a number on a screen. It's yours; you earned every hour. So why would anyone hand back a tenth? Go back to Jacob, running from his brother, asleep on the ground with a stone under his head. He dreams of a ladder with angels going up and down, and wakes up shaken. He owns nothing but what he's carrying. Then he makes a promise about money he doesn't have yet. In the JPS 1917 translation: "of all that Thou shalt give me I will surely give the tenth unto Thee."
screen: `A FIRST PAYCHECK.` → `JACOB, ON THE RUN.` → `"I WILL SURELY GIVE THE TENTH."`

segments.voice: Listen for the word give, twice. Jacob calls everything he'll ever earn something given, and the tenth is his way of saying so out loud. In the Torah, tithes were harvests: grain, wine and oil set apart, and in the third year a tithe left in town for the Levite, the stranger, the orphan and the widow, so they could eat and be satisfied. Later teachers carried the tenth over to money. It's called ma'aser kesafim, a tenth of money, and teachers differ on whether it's a law or a strong custom. The Shulchan Aruch, a code of Jewish law, lays out a scale: up to a fifth is the finest way to give, a tenth is the middle way, and less than that is a stingy eye. Here's what a tenth can do that a good mood can't. It's a number, so it doesn't wait until you feel generous. It shrinks when you earn little and grows when you earn more. And it comes off the top, before the money is spent, so what you give isn't leftovers. Something to tell a friend tonight: Jacob made this promise before he had a single thing to tithe.
screen: `ALL THAT THOU SHALT GIVE ME.` · `HARVESTS FOR THE STRANGER AND THE WIDOW.` · `A FIFTH, A TENTH, A STINGY EYE.` · `OFF THE TOP, NOT LEFTOVERS.` · then, large: `GIVE A TENTH.`

segments.voice: Set out ten small things in a row: coins, beans, paper clips. Touch each one as you count it, and feel how alike they are. Then slide one a little apart from the others, and rest your eyes on the nine still in front of you, and the one that already belongs to someone else.
screen: `TEN SMALL THINGS.` · `TOUCH EACH ONE.` · `SLIDE ONE APART.`

segments.voice: Ma'aser: a tenth, set apart first. In the Torah, a tenth of the harvest; later, a tenth of money, given to tzedakah.
For your pocket: give a tenth, off the top, the way Jacob promised with empty hands. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many observant Jews set aside ma'aser, a tenth of their income, for tzedakah; some keep a separate account or jar for it and decide during the year where it goes.
